title: Major issues on Code of Conduct settled – Marcos
summary: Although a binding code of conduct for South China Sea claimants was not completed under the Philippines’ chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, President Marcos said the…

blocks.text: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. speaks during a press briefing at the International Media Center in Pasay City on November 17, 2026

MANILA, Philippines — Although a binding code of conduct for South China Sea claimants was not completed under the Philippines’ chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), President Marcos said the major issues surrounding the proposed rules have been settled.

At a media briefing after the ASEAN Summit closing ceremony, Marcos quoted Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro as saying that 85 to 90 percent of the code of conduct “has actually been done.”

“We had, of course, hoped that during the chairship of the Philippines, that we would be able to announce that the COC (code of conduct) was finished. However, that’s not the case,” the President told reporters at the International Media Center in Pasay.
“But we can take solace in the fact that the majority of the issues – actually, the large issues – are already done and decided and agreed upon,” he added.
Marcos said negotiators still have to thresh out the definition of terms to make the code comprehensible to all parties.

“There are definitions, and there are phrases, and there are paragraphs that need to be clearly defined, so that it is very understandable, and it is very clear to everyone involved that these are the rules, these are the understood and accepted mores and norms that we will all be following,” the Chief Executive said.
Marcos thanked the ASEAN members and China for their participation in crafting the binding code of conduct, saying “everyone has worked hard to bring us to the point that we are in now.”

He said there was a tacit agreement that the parties would abide by the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), a non-binding document adopted in 2002 to prevent tensions in the strategic sea lane. “Until the COC is ready, until it is finalized, until it is signed by all parties – by ASEAN, by China – then we pledge to continue to follow on the DOC’s guidance,” Marcos said.

“ASEAN and China reaffirmed firm commitments to sustaining the effort, towards the conclusion of the final phase of negotiations, or a substantive and effective COC, consistent with UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea), and it effectively will govern the behavior of parties at sea,” he added.
